Jehoiakim Procures His Own Ruin.<div eID="gen5124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5125" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3596"/><hi type="bold">1-2. Nebuchadnezzar--</hi>the son of Nabopolassar, the founder of the Chaldee monarchy. This invasion took place in the fourth year of Jehoiakim's, and the first of Nebuchadnezzar's reign (<reference osisRef="Jer.25.1">Jr 25:1</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Jer.46.2">Jr 46:2</reference>). The young king of Assyria being probably detained at home on account of his father's demise, despatched, along with the Chaldean troops on his border, an army composed of the tributary nations that were contiguous to Judea, to chastise Jehoiakim's revolt from his yoke. But this hostile band was only an instrument in executing the divine judgment (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.2">2Ki 24:2</reference>) denounced by the prophets against Judah for the sins of the people; and hence, though marching by the orders of the Assyrian monarch, they are described as sent by the Lord (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.3">2Ki 24:3</reference>). <div eID="gen5125" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3602"/><div sID="gen5135" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3602"/><hi type="bold">10-13. At that time--</hi>within three months after his accession to the throne. It was the spring of the year (<reference osisRef="2Chr.36.10">2Ch 36:10</reference>); so early did he indicate a feeling hostile to the interests of his Assyrian liege lord, by forming a league with Egypt. Nebuchadnezzar sent his generals to besiege Jerusalem, as Jeremiah had foretold (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.28">Jr 22:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.34.20">34:20</reference>), and soon after he followed in person. Convinced of the hopelessness of making any effectual resistance, Jehoiachin, going to the camp of the besiegers, surrendered (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.24.12">2Ki 24:12</reference>), in the expectation, probably, of being allowed to retain his throne as a vassal of the Assyrian empire. But Nebuchadnezzar's clemency towards the kings of Judah was now exhausted, so that Jehoiachin was sent as a captive to Babylon, according to Jeremiah's prediction (<reference osisRef="Jer.22.24">Jr 22:24</reference>), accompanied by the queen mother (the same who had held that dignity under Jehoahaz) (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.31">2Ki 23:31</reference>), his generals, and officers. This happened in the eighth year of Nebuchadnezzar's reign, computing from the time when he was associated with his father in the government. Those that were left consisted chiefly of the poorer sort of people and the unskilled workmen. The palace and the temple were ransacked. The smaller golden vessels had been taken on the first capture of Jerusalem and placed by Nebuchadnezzar in the temple of his god as tokens of victory. They were used by Belshazzar at his impious feast [Da 5:2], for the purpose of rewarding his army with these trophies, among which were probably the golden candlesticks, the ark, &c. (compare <reference osisRef="2Chr.36.7">2Ch 36:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.1.2">Da 1:2</reference>). Now the gold plating was torn off all the larger temple furniture. <div eID="gen5135" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_plain: 17-19. the king of Babylon made Mattaniah, his father's brother, king in his stead-- Adhering to his former policy of maintaining a show of monarchy, Nebuchadnezzar appointed the third and youngest son of Josiah ( 1Ch 3:15 ), full brother of Jehoahaz, and uncle of the captive Jehoiachin. But, according to the custom of conquerors, who changed the names of the great men they took captives in war, in token of their supremacy, he gave him the new name of Zedekiah-- that is, "The righteous of God." This being a purely Hebrew name, it seems that he allowed the puppet king to choose his own name, which was confirmed. His heart towards God was the same as that of Jehoiakim, impenitent and heedless of God's word.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3605"/><div sID="gen5140" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3605"/><hi type="bold">20. through the anger of the Lord ... he cast them out from his presence--</hi>that is, in the course of God's righteous providence, his policy as king would prove ruinous to his country.<div eID="gen5140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5141" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon--</hi>instigated by ambassadors from the neighboring states who came to congratulate him on his ascension to the throne (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.17.3">Jr 17:3</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Jer.28.1">Jr 28:1</reference>), and at the same time get him to join them in a common league to throw off the Assyrian yoke. Though warned by Jeremiah against this step, the infatuated and perjured (<reference osisRef="Ezek.17.13">Eze 17:13</reference>) Zedekiah persisted in his revolt. <chapter eID="2Kgs.24"/>

Though warned by Jeremiah against this step, the infatuated and perjured ( Eze 17:13 ) Zedekiah persisted in his revolt.
